turns.output: In our family, the first sign of chicken adobo isn’t the smell of garlic or the rattle of the pot lid. It’s someone asking, “Did you start the rice?” Nobody wants to get to the table and find there’s nothing to soak up the sauce. My grandmother made hers with bone-in chicken, whole peppercorns, and a bay leaf she always seemed to find on her own plate. She measured the soy sauce and vinegar in a chipped teacup, but she judged the balance by tasting a spoonful of sauce over rice. That’s the part of her recipe I hope you’ll keep, whatever you use to measure. The sauce should be tangy enough to make you want another bite of chicken, and savory enough to make plain rice feel like a treat. If there’s any left tomorrow, call me. I’ll bring the rice and a couple of fried eggs for our breakfast.

In our family, chicken adobo announces dinner long before anyone calls us to the table. First comes the sharp smell of vinegar, then the garlic, and finally someone lifting the lid to ask if the rice is ready. My grandmother made hers in a pot with one loose handle. She never bothered to fix it, but she always remembered who liked a drumstick and who wanted extra sauce. This recipe is our best attempt to put her handfuls and splashes into words. The chicken should be tender enough to pull from the bone with a fork, and the sauce should leave you looking for one more spoonful of rice. Make it when everyone is home, or when you wish they were. If there is any left for breakfast, warm it in a pan and fry an egg. In our house, that was always the reward for washing the dinner dishes.

Welcome to this week’s field notes on AI tools. The best part of trying something new is the moment you stop thinking about the tool and get back to what you meant to do. Maybe that’s finding the one decision buried in a meeting transcript. Maybe it’s hearing how a paragraph sounds before you send it to your editor.

This week, we’re looking at three new tools through that lens: a voice notebook for ideas that arrive on a walk, a research assistant that shows its sources, and an image editor for the small fixes that somehow eat an afternoon. For each one, we’ll ask what it does well, where it needs supervision, and whether it’s worth making room for.

First up: the voice notebook. A grocery list is easy. The real test is whether it can untangle a rambling thought without tidying away the bit that made it interesting.

The sky is blue because air scatters sunlight, and it scatters some colors more than others.

Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mix of colors, as you can see in a rainbow. Each color travels as a light wave. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, which means the distance from one wave crest to the next is smaller.

As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, it meets molecules of gases like nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter some of the light, sending it off in new directions. They scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. So when you look at a patch of sky away from the Sun, much of the light reaching your eyes is blue light that has changed direction. Violet light scatters even more strongly, but our eyes are less sensitive to violet, so the sky looks blue rather than violet.

The same idea explains a red sunset. When the Sun is near the horizon, its light travels through more air before reaching you. Much of the blue light gets scattered out of that direct path, leaving the sunlight you see richer in reds and oranges.

Sunlight looks white, but it contains all the colors of the rainbow. Light travels in waves, and each color has a different wavelength. A wavelength is the distance from one wave crest to the next. Blue and violet light have shorter wavelengths than red and orange light.

On its way to the ground, sunlight passes through air made of tiny molecules. Those molecules scatter some of the light, sending it in new directions. They scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. So when you look at a patch of sky far from the Sun, much of the light reaching your eyes is blue light that changed direction on its journey.

If violet has an even shorter wavelength than blue, why isn't the sky violet? There is less violet than blue in sunlight, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. We see the mix of scattered colors as blue.

The same idea helps explain sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light travels through a much longer stretch of air to reach you. Much of the blue light scatters out of that path, leaving the light that reaches you directly looking orange or red.

A browser cache is a temporary storage space where your browser keeps copies of things it downloads, such as images, fonts, and files that control how a web page looks.

Imagine visiting a website for the first time. To show you the site’s logo, your browser asks the website’s server to send the image. The browser displays it and may save a copy in the cache. When you open another page on the same site, your browser can use the saved logo instead of downloading it again. That helps the page load faster and uses less data.

But what if the website changes its logo? When the server sends the image, it can tell the browser how long to treat the copy as fresh. After that time, the browser can ask, “Has this image changed?” If not, the browser keeps using its copy. If it has changed, the server sends the new image.

You can clear the cache in your browser settings. This sometimes fixes a page that looks wrong because of an outdated file. The next visit may be slower, though, because your browser has to download those files again.

A browser cache is a place on your device where your browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit. Think of it like keeping a cookbook in your kitchen. If you want to read the same recipe tomorrow, you can open the book instead of making another trip to the library.

When you first visit a website, your browser asks the website’s server for the files it needs to show the page. These might include text, images, and instructions that control how the page looks. The browser can save some of those files in its cache.

Suppose you open a second page on the same website. If both pages use the same logo, your browser may already have a copy. It can display that copy without downloading the image again. This helps the page load faster and uses less data.

A website can tell your browser how long to reuse a file before checking for changes. When that time is up, the browser can ask the server whether the file has changed. If it has, the browser downloads the new version. If not, it keeps using the copy it already has.

Dear Hiring Team,

The first time I watched a designer use a component I had built, she tried to drag a handle that I had made purely decorative. She was right: it looked draggable. I changed it that afternoon, and the conversation that followed was more useful than the original spec. That’s the kind of work I want to do at your startup: build tools that respond to the way people actually design.

In my current role, I work with two product designers on a shared React and TypeScript component library. Recently, we rebuilt a color picker that lost the user’s selection whenever a preview refreshed. I traced the problem to how we stored draft state, then sat with a designer to test the fix across mouse, keyboard, and touch input. The best sign that it worked was that our next feedback session was about color, not the picker.

I’d bring that same attention to the editing experience on your team. I enjoy the technical work of keeping a canvas responsive, but I’m just as interested in what happens when someone pauses, undoes a change, or reaches for a shortcut. Those moments tell me what we should be building next.

For fifteen years, you were the sound of home: nails clicking down the hallway, a tail thumping against the cupboard, one hopeful bark when the cheese drawer opened. You knew which child would drop a crust and which grownup needed company on the porch. When the children left for college, you kept watch over their rooms. When they came back, you greeted them with the same ridiculous spin, even after your hips insisted on a slower version.

In your last summer we took our walks at your pace. We learned how much there was to notice between our gate and the corner. Now the leash hangs still, and somebody always looks down before opening that drawer. We miss you in a hundred ordinary moments. What a gift it was to have so many of them together, sweet friend. This house will always be the house where you grew old, loved.

For fifteen years you knew the sound of every footstep in this house. You could tell who was coming home by the turn of a key, and you always brought a sock to the door, as if none of us could be trusted to have packed one.

You were there when the children took their first steps, and still there when they came home from college. By then your muzzle was white, and we had learned to take the long way slowly, stopping at the hedge where the sparrows lived.

This morning we found a tennis ball beneath the lilacs. For a moment we expected to hear you crashing through the leaves to claim it. We left it there. Thank you for all the ordinary days you made dear to us. What a gift it was to be the people you were so glad to see come through that door.

At 40, you are not starting from zero. You are starting with years of asking questions, solving problems, and figuring things out when the instructions made no sense. Those habits belong at a keyboard, too.

Pick one small thing you wish a computer would do for you. Maybe it’s totaling your grocery bill or choosing dinner from a list of favorites. Write a few lines. Run them. If something breaks, take a breath and read the message. An error is a clue, not a verdict.

Some days, progress will look like building something that works. Other days, it will look like understanding why yesterday’s attempt didn’t. Both count. Keep a note of the things that once puzzled you; soon enough, you’ll catch yourself explaining one to somebody else.

You don’t have to catch up with anyone. You get to make something that wasn’t there before. Start small, and start today.

At 40, you already know something every programmer needs to learn: being confused is not the same as being incapable. Think of all the things that once took your full attention and now feel ordinary. Coding can become one of them.

Start with something you want, even if it seems small. Write a program that picks dinner from your favorite recipes. When it suggests tacos five nights in a row, laugh, then find out why. That moment of curiosity will teach you more than trying to look like someone who knows what they are doing.

Give yourself twenty minutes today. Tomorrow, change one thing and see what happens. Keep your first attempts so you can look back when progress feels slow.

You do not need to catch up with anyone. You get to make things that did not exist before you sat down. That is a fine reason to begin.

At low tide, the island gave back things it had no use for: a boot without its fellow, the brass head of a bedstead, once a sheep so perfectly preserved in salt that Miriam had apologized before touching it.

That morning it gave back a telephone.

She heard it from the lantern room, six flights above the rocks. Two short rings, a pause, then one long. Her mother used to ring like that on the party line, back when a person could announce herself by the shape of an interruption.

Miriam took the stairs in her slippers.

The telephone sat upright in a patch of bladderwrack. It was green, with a rotary dial and a little paper circle in the middle where somebody had written HOME. Its cord trailed into a crevice. Each time it rang, a shrimp flicked backward through the pool beside it.

She let it ring once more. For twenty years she had imagined what she might say if given another minute with her mother. Now all she could think was that her feet were wet.

She lifted the receiver.

“Miriam?” said a child's voice.

“Yes.”

“It's me. I'm in the cupboard. You said you'd count to a hundred.”

The phone began ringing at low tide, just as Ada was carrying the kitchen chair back indoors. She had spent the afternoon on it, painting the lighthouse door a yellow nobody on the mainland had approved.

At first she thought the sound came from her pocket. Then she remembered where she had left her mobile, in a jar of rice after yesterday's incident with the soup.

She set down the chair.

Below the landing steps, on a shelf of black rock still glossy with seawater, stood a green telephone. It was the heavy kind, with a dial and a cloth cord. The cord trailed into a pool where three little prawns were picking at it.

Ada went down in her painty slippers. By the time she reached the shelf, the ringing had stopped.

“Typical,” she said.

She lifted the receiver anyway. There was no dial tone, only the domestic sound of somebody scraping toast over a sink.

“Mum?” said a boy.

Ada sat down on the wet rock. For thirty years she had tried to remember his voice without the help of the tape they had played at the inquest.

“I'm here,” she said.

“Good. Can you come and get me?”

A year into engineering management, the habit I’ve worked hardest to break is saying, “I’ll take a look,” when I really mean, “I’ll take over.”

As an engineer, that impulse often helped me get things done. As a manager, it sometimes left a teammate waiting for my answer when they were perfectly capable of finding their own. Now I try to ask, “Would it help to talk it through, or do you need me to make a decision?” The distinction matters.

I’ve also learned to save status updates for writing when I can. It leaves room in one-on-ones for the things that rarely make it onto a project board: an ownership question, a disagreement about a design, or work someone wants to try next.

My favorite moment this year was watching a teammate lead a design review I once would have run. I learned something from how they did it.

In my first year as an engineering manager, I opened my editor more than once when what my team actually needed was a decision.

One afternoon, two engineers walked me through different approaches to a migration. I started sketching a third. Then one of them asked, “Which matters more here, the launch date or making this easy to reverse?” That was the part they needed me to own. Once I clarified the priority, they had a plan by lunch.

Since then, I try to ask one question before offering advice: “What do you need from me?” Sometimes it’s technical feedback. Sometimes it’s a decision, an introduction, or ten minutes to think out loud with someone who knows the context.

I still love writing code. What changed this year is that I no longer measure a good week by how often I got to do it.

In Jane Austen’s *Pride and Prejudice*, Elizabeth Bennet’s mother wants to see all five of her daughters married: the family estate will pass to a male cousin, leaving them with little financial security. When the wealthy Charles Bingley rents a nearby house, he and Elizabeth’s sister Jane fall in love. Bingley’s friend, Mr. Darcy, makes a worse impression. Elizabeth overhears him dismiss her as a potential dance partner, so she readily believes a charming officer’s account of his cruelty.

Darcy falls in love with Elizabeth, but his proposal dwells so much on her family’s inferiority that she rejects him. A letter from Darcy exposes the officer’s dishonesty. Later, when that same officer runs away with Elizabeth’s youngest sister, Darcy quietly helps arrange their marriage, sparing the Bennets public disgrace. His discretion does more to change Elizabeth’s feelings than his declaration of love did. In time, both Jane and Elizabeth marry the men they love.

Austen gives the title’s faults to both protagonists: Darcy’s pride distorts his judgment of Elizabeth’s family, while Elizabeth takes pride in her ability to judge character. Their romance turns on a difficult achievement for two intelligent people: each learns to admit being wrong.

In Jane Austen’s *Pride and Prejudice*, the arrival of two wealthy bachelors excites the Bennet household, where five daughters stand to lose their home when their father dies. Jane, the eldest, falls in love with the amiable Charles Bingley. Her sister Elizabeth takes an immediate dislike to his friend Mr. Darcy after overhearing him dismiss her at a dance. When Darcy proposes to Elizabeth, he dwells on her family’s social inferiority even as he declares his love. She refuses him, accusing him of separating Jane from Bingley and of mistreating a charming officer named Wickham.

A letter from Darcy forces Elizabeth to reconsider what she knows about both men. Later, when her younger sister Lydia runs away with Wickham, Darcy quietly helps arrange their marriage, sparing the Bennets a public disgrace. Bingley returns to Jane, and Elizabeth accepts Darcy’s second proposal, offered this time with genuine humility.

Austen makes changing one’s mind a central act of love. Elizabeth learns how readily wounded pride can pass for sound judgment; Darcy learns that good intentions do not excuse contempt. Their growing respect offers a hopeful contrast to a marriage market in which a woman’s financial security can depend on whose proposal she accepts.

When Johannes Gutenberg developed his printing system in Mainz around 1450, European scribes still copied most books by hand. His use of movable metal type allowed a printer to arrange letters for a page, print hundreds of copies, and then reuse the letters for another page. Books became cheaper, and readers in distant cities could consult the same text or diagram. Scholars could compare observations, spot errors, and publish corrections for others to examine.

The press also changed who could take part in public debate. During the Reformation, printers distributed Martin Luther’s arguments in short German pamphlets. Readers did not need to know Latin to follow the dispute, and people who could not read could hear a pamphlet read aloud. Catholic writers used the same presses to answer Luther, so printing widened the controversy rather than simply handing victory to one side.

Over time, printing expanded the market for writing in European languages and helped standardize spelling. It did not make everyone literate or everything in print reliable: a false rumor could travel as readily as a discovery. What changed was the scale and speed at which Europeans could share ideas, argue over them, and build on them.

The printing press changed Europe by making written works cheaper to copy and easier to share. Before Johannes Gutenberg developed his system of movable type in Mainz around 1450, most books in Europe were copied by hand. A scribe might spend months producing one volume. Once a printer had set a page in type, a press crew could produce hundreds of copies of that page in a day.

That difference in scale mattered during the Reformation. When Martin Luther challenged church practices in 1517, printers quickly circulated his arguments in short pamphlets. Many were in German rather than Latin, so readers outside universities and the clergy could follow the debate. Even people who could not read could hear a pamphlet read aloud at home or in a tavern.

Print also changed how people learned from one another. Scholars in different cities could examine copies of the same anatomical illustration, point out an error, and see it corrected in a later edition. Merchants could learn arithmetic from printed manuals, and children could practice reading with inexpensive primers. The press did not make every claim true, but it gave far more Europeans the chance to encounter an idea, question it, and pass it on.

By the time I reached the Ferry Building, the rain had found the gap between my collar and my scarf. Inside, I bought a cup of coffee and a pear so ripe the vendor handed me a second napkin. For a while I stood under the arcade watching commuters negotiate the puddles, each convinced of a slightly different route to dry land. When the downpour eased, I walked up Columbus Avenue to City Lights, where my shoes squeaked so loudly on the stairs that a reader in the poetry room looked up and grinned. I spent an hour there and left with a slim paperback tucked inside my coat. By then the windows of North Beach were steaming up for lunch. At a counter facing the street, I ate a square of focaccia and watched a man across the way tip an awning full of water onto his own boots. He laughed before anyone else could. I had meant to spend the afternoon photographing the Golden Gate Bridge. Instead, I rode the bus back with wet socks, a book of poems, and the smell of rosemary on my fingers. I never did get a photograph, but I remember that lunch.

Rain found me halfway up Sacramento Street, just as I was congratulating myself on leaving my umbrella at the hotel. I ducked into a Chinatown bakery, bought a warm pineapple bun, and stood by the window pulling its crumbly top apart one piece at a time. Outside, a woman tipped water from the awning of her vegetable stall with a broom, then went right back to arranging oranges. By noon I had stopped trying to stay dry. I walked down to the Ferry Building, where the bay had turned the color of a nickel and a gull was making off with somebody's lunch. From a bench under the arcade, I watched a ferry nose into its berth. The passengers came ashore in bright jackets, looking considerably better prepared than I was. My favorite moment came later, aboard a California Street cable car. At the crest of the hill, the gripman rang the bell for a driver who had paused in the tracks. The driver waved, the car rolled on, and for one clear second I could see all the way back to the water. My socks were soaked. I stayed on the outside bench until it was time to get off.

The broth is what I’ll remember about this little ramen shop. It arrived steaming, with tiny beads of oil on the surface and a roasted garlic aroma that made me put my phone away. Rich without being heavy, it had enough depth to keep me reaching for the spoon long after the springy noodles were gone. The pork was tender, and the egg had the soft, amber center I always hope for.

Getting that bowl, though, took nearly forty minutes on a Tuesday evening. Our server was friendly when we caught her eye, but nobody mentioned the delay, and our tea sat empty through most of the wait. I’d gladly come back for that broth, just not on a lunch break or before a movie. Bring someone you like talking to, order as soon as you sit down, and leave yourself time to enjoy the bowl when it finally lands.

I would come back to this ramen shop for the broth alone. My bowl arrived under a cloud of steam, with little beads of garlic oil floating on a rich, cloudy surface. The first spoonful tasted deeply of pork, and a bite of fresh scallion kept the next one from feeling too heavy. Springy noodles held their chew to the bottom of the bowl.

Unfortunately, I had plenty of time to admire everyone else's dinner before mine appeared. It took fifteen minutes to place an order and another thirty to get our food. My friend's ramen came out first; by the time I picked up my chopsticks, she was fishing for her last noodle. Our server apologized and brought us fresh tea without being asked, which helped.

Go on a quiet evening with someone you enjoy talking to. For a quick lunch, I would try somewhere else on the block.

Budgeting App 2.0 makes it easier to see what you can spend before your next paycheck. The redesigned dashboard shows your account balances alongside upcoming bills and the amount left in each budget category. You can pin the categories you check most often, so your grocery budget is right there when you need it.

Budgets are more flexible, too. Choose a monthly or payday-based schedule, and set a rollover rule for each category. If you spend less than planned on dining out, you can carry the difference into the next period without changing how your other budgets work.

When plans change, you can now move money between categories without editing your original targets. A new monthly summary shows those adjustments alongside your spending, so you can tell whether a higher grocery total was a one-time expense or a good reason to adjust next month’s budget.

Version 2.0 makes it easier to plan for the month ahead and adjust when life gets expensive. The redesigned home screen shows how much you have left to spend after upcoming bills and savings contributions are set aside. Tap that amount to see the calculation, so you can decide whether dinner out fits the plan.

You can now give each savings goal a target date. Whether you are planning a trip or replacing a laptop, the app shows how much to set aside each month and updates that amount when you make a contribution. If your priorities change, you can move money between budget categories without editing your past transactions.

Finding a purchase is easier, too. Search by merchant, amount, or note, then narrow the results to a single category. Your existing budgets, categories, and transaction history carry over automatically when you update to version 2.0.

On balance, remote work helps junior engineers when teams make it easy to ask questions. At home, a new engineer can pause a recorded walkthrough, try the example, and return to the part that makes sense only after something breaks. A thoughtful comment on a pull request can teach a lesson they’ll use long after they’ve forgotten the change that prompted it. Yet remote work also makes it remarkably easy to spend an afternoon stuck on a problem a teammate could explain in two minutes. In an office, a junior engineer might overhear a colleague mention that the test suite sometimes fails for reasons unrelated to the code. At home, they may read that same failure as evidence that they’ve misunderstood the assignment. That’s why I’d rather start my career on a remote team that pairs on tricky tasks than in an office where everyone wears headphones and the manager is always busy. The best mentor I can imagine is someone who makes time to hear what I tried, shows me how they’d investigate, and lets me finish the fix. Whether that conversation happens across a desk or on a call matters less than whether I can count on it happening.

On balance, I think remote work helps junior engineers, but only when their managers treat learning as part of the job rather than something that happens by proximity. Consider what happens when a new engineer gets stuck on a failing test. In an office, a colleague might notice the puzzled look and pull up a chair. At home, the engineer can spend an afternoon worrying that a question will make them look incompetent. The difference is not the distance itself but whether the team has made asking for help feel ordinary. A mentor who invites a junior colleague to share a screen can do more than fix the test. By explaining which clues matter and which ones to ignore, the mentor makes a usually invisible skill available to someone else. Remote work also gives beginners room to read unfamiliar code without feeling that every quiet minute needs an explanation. That freedom to concentrate is worth preserving at any level. Still, I would advise a graduate choosing between two offers to ask each manager about the last engineer they trained. A specific story about a mistake, a conversation, and a lesson tells you more than any policy about where people sit.

Running and swimming both build cardiovascular endurance, but they challenge the body in different ways. Running is a weight-bearing activity: each stride loads the legs and hips, which can help maintain bone strength. It’s also convenient. With comfortable shoes and a safe route, you can fit a short run into a busy day. The trade-off is impact. If you’re new to running, alternating walking and jogging can make it easier to build endurance without doing too much too soon.

Swimming uses the shoulders, back, and core as well as the legs. Because water supports your weight, it puts less stress on the joints and may be more comfortable if running bothers your knees or hips. Its main drawbacks are access and technique: you need a safe place to swim, and learning to coordinate your breathing with your stroke can take practice.

For general fitness, how regularly you exercise matters more than which activity you choose. If you enjoy being outdoors and want a workout that starts at your door, running may suit you better. If you prefer the water and want a low-impact workout, try swimming. Alternating the two gives you variety without having to choose a favorite.

Running and swimming both build cardiovascular endurance, but they place different demands on your body and your schedule. Running is easy to fit into a busy day because, with a comfortable pair of shoes and a safe route, you can start from your front door. It strengthens your legs, and the impact of each stride helps maintain bone strength. That same impact can make running uncomfortable if you have joint pain. If you are new to it, alternating short runs with walking can help you build endurance gradually.

Swimming works your shoulders, back, core, and legs while the water supports your weight. This makes it a useful choice if you want a vigorous workout with less stress on your joints. The main obstacles are access and technique. You need a pool or a safe place to swim, and learning to coordinate your breathing with your strokes can take practice.

Both activities can be gentle or demanding, depending on your pace. If convenience matters most, running may be easier to sustain. If you enjoy the water or find impact uncomfortable, swimming may suit you better. If you like both, alternating them adds variety and gives your legs a break from impact.

1/5 Simple code beats clever code because writing it is only the first job. Someone still has to review it, debug it, and change it. Often that someone is you, six months later.

2/5 Short isn’t the same as simple. A one-liner that makes you mentally unpack three transformations isn’t saving much. Give the intermediate result a name. `overdueInvoices` tells the reader something the line count can’t.

3/5 Simple code makes debugging easier. If a total looks wrong, it helps to inspect the subtotal, discount, and tax separately instead of untangling one expression while a customer waits.

4/5 Solve today’s problem directly. Two shipping rules might need an `if`, not a rules engine. If more rules arrive, you’ll have real examples to guide the design instead of guesses about what they might be.

5/5 Cleverness earns its place when it buys something real. If a tricky lookup takes a request from 2 seconds to 20 milliseconds, keep it, test it, and explain why it’s there. Otherwise, choose the version nobody has to decode.

1/5 Clever code makes sense when the trick is fresh in your head. Simple code still makes sense six months later, when you open the file to fix something else.

2/5 Give business rules names. `if can_refund(order):` tells the reader what decision is being made. Anyone who needs the details knows where to look.

3/5 A few intermediate variables can make a bug easier to find. If a total looks wrong, you can inspect the subtotal, discount, and tax instead of untangling one long expression.

4/5 Sometimes the clever version earns its place. If a benchmark shows that a loop is too slow, optimize it. Leave a comment explaining why the obvious version wasn't enough.

5/5 A useful code review question: “If the rule changed tomorrow, would I know what to edit?” That's a better test of simplicity than counting lines.

Maya Chen is a software engineer who builds tools that help developers spend less time debugging and more time making things. She began baking sourdough after a production bug convinced her she needed a hobby with no screens. Her first loaf was dense enough to prop open a door, but keeping notes on each bake turned out to be as useful as reading logs. Today, Maya mentors engineers, maintains an open-source testing library, and brings a still-warm loaf to her team’s monthly breakfast. In her talks, she draws on both crafts to explore how small experiments lead to better decisions. Ask her about flaky tests, late-night releases, or the jar of starter that has followed her through three apartment moves.

Maya Patel is a software engineer who builds tools that help public librarians spend less time wrestling with databases and more time with readers. She came to programming through a summer job at her neighborhood branch, where she wrote a script to rescue a decade of book club records. Outside work, Maya bakes sourdough in a small kitchen with an oven that runs hot on the left. Her baking notebook holds sketches of lopsided loaves alongside the names of neighbors who ate them. In her talk, Maya shares what both pursuits have taught her about keeping useful notes, asking better questions, and knowing when to leave a promising experiment alone. She welcomes questions about debugging or getting a crisp crust.

To my oldest friend and the love of your life: I’ve been saving this toast since we were twelve, though the original draft had considerably more jokes about braces.

I knew this was serious when you called after your first date. Usually you give me the highlights. That night I got the whole story, right down to the song playing while you waited for the bus. You wanted to remember absolutely everything.

Watching you together now, I think that’s your gift to each other. You pay attention. You know when to put the kettle on, when to ask another question, and when a truly terrible pun deserves a second telling.

So here’s to a lifetime of noticing: the good songs, the small kindnesses, the look across a crowded room that says, “Wait until we get home; I have a story.” May you always want to hear the whole thing. Cheers!

When Sam and I were eight, we buried a tin of treasures behind my parents' garage. I contributed three marbles. Sam contributed a note reminding us where we'd buried it, which unfortunately went inside the tin. That's my oldest friend: always trying to look after everyone, occasionally overlooking a detail.

Years later, when Sam first brought Jamie over for dinner, I watched them washing dishes together. Jamie washed, Sam dried, and both sang the wrong words to the same song. I remember standing in the doorway, thinking I could go sit down. My friend was home.

Sam and Jamie, may you have a lifetime of kitchens filled with music, friends who stay for dessert, and small discoveries worth saving. And if you ever bury a time capsule, please let Jamie keep the map.

Everyone, raise a glass to my oldest friend and the love who knows the wrong words too.
